result: The authors developed and optimized a nanobody generation pipeline using affinity purification, LC-MS/MS, and CDR clustering to identify 180 high-confidence candidates, of which 138 were validated by binding screens and 116 were selected for detailed characterization. The pipeline demonstrated high diversity with minimal overlap between S1 and S2 binders and between animals.
evaluation: Reviewers praised the manuscript as describing 'an impressive collection of hundreds of new nanobodies' and providing 'a comprehensive characterization of a repertoire.' No concerns were raised about the pipeline methodology or the diversity of candidates generated.

result: All 116 characterized nanobodies bound with high affinity (>60% with KD < 1 nM, two with picomolar affinities), with fast association rates (many kon ≥ 10^6) surpassing typical monoclonal antibodies. The distribution showed 71 RBD binders, 19 non-RBD S1 binders, and 26 S2 binders, with no obvious bias in affinities across domains.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the work provides 'comprehensive characterization' with 'complementary biophysical...assays.' Reviewer 1 requested clarification on normalization methods for binding assays but did not challenge the affinity data itself.

result: Six of seven tested nanobodies retained strong binding to both Alpha and Beta variants, with S1-23 showing reduced but respectable binding to Alpha (KD 17 pM to 230 pM) but abolished binding to Beta. Off rates were most affected by variant mutations.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the variant binding data. Reviewer 2 noted 'it would be desirable...if at least some data on the now dominating Delta variant was included,' indicating the data presented is accepted but could be expanded.

result: Nanobodies demonstrated thermal stability (Tm 50-80°C) and freeze-drying without cryoprotectants had no significant effect on stability, kinetics, or affinity.
evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the stability data. The findings align with the reviewers' acknowledgment of the work's 'comprehensive characterization' of nanobody properties.

result: Epitope binning revealed at least eight RBD epitope bins, four S1-non-RBD bins, and five S2 bins. Mass photometry demonstrated at least three different nanobodies can bind simultaneously to the RBD.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the work 'defines epitopes on the RBD or spike' with impressive detail. Reviewer 2 suggested comparing defined epitopes with those from other studies (Sun et al., Koenig et al.), indicating acceptance of the data but requesting additional context.

result: 36% of monomeric nanobodies neutralized with IC50s ≤100 nM, with 17 potent neutralizers at ≤20 nM. The most potent neutralizers mapped to RBD, but importantly, nanobodies binding outside the RBD (S1 non-RBD and S2) also showed neutralizing activity—the first such evidence for nanobodies.
evaluation: Reviewers praised the work for identifying 'non-receptor binding domain nanobodies' as a significant contribution. Reviewer 2 requested comparison with benchmark nanobodies and clarification of their identities, but did not challenge the neutralization data itself.

result: Oligomerization significantly improved IC50s and affinities for most nanobodies, with dramatic improvements observed (e.g., S1-RBD-35: 12 nM to 70 pM for trimer; S2-7 converted from non-neutralizer to IC50 ~30 nM). However, enhancement was not universal and must be determined empirically.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged 'extensive bioengineering to substantially improve potency.' Reviewer 2 noted this concept has been applied to SARS-CoV-2 nanobodies by others and requested citation, but did not challenge the findings.

result: Seven of 27 tested anti-RBD nanobodies displayed excellent neutralizing activity against SARS-CoV-1 pseudovirus, with some showing similar IC50s against both SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV-1. Three of 11 non-RBD binders also neutralized SARS-CoV-1.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the cross-neutralization data. The findings contribute to the overall assessment that the work provides 'significant impacts on SARS-CoV-2 research and therapeutics.'

result: All tested nanobodies that neutralized pseudovirus also showed potent neutralization in authentic virus assays (plaque/focus reduction) and ALI cultures. S1-1 potently neutralized at all concentrations tested, while S1-23 showed dose-dependent inhibition with enhanced efficacy as a trimer.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the authentic virus neutralization data. Reviewer 1 requested clarification that the ALI model does not truly 'mimic a treatment regimen' since nanobodies were added before and after infection, but this is a presentation issue rather than a challenge to the data validity.

result: 32 unique escape mutants were identified for 22 representative nanobodies, with some selecting mutations at positions known from human antibody studies (e.g., E484K) and others at novel positions. Combining two nanobodies in cocktails prevented escape in 8 of 9 cases, elevating the genetic barrier for resistance.
evaluation: Reviewers praised the work for demonstrating 'resistance to escaping variants' and 'synergistic activities using nanobody cocktails.' Reviewer 2 requested citation of the first study using similar evolution experiments (Baum et al.), but did not challenge the findings.

result: Integrative modeling using IMP with restraints from escape mutant data and XL-MS generated structures for 21 neutralizing nanobodies classified into 10 groups. The repertoire explores much of the available epitope space, with ~80% of anti-RBD, ~60% of non-RBD S1, and ~20% of S2 nanobodies being neutralizing. The first neutralizing S2-binding nanobodies are presented.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 expressed concern about reliance on IMP modeling for identifying unique binding sites and variant resistance, requesting validation with a structurally characterized nanobody as a control or justification for why this would not be appropriate. The reviewer noted 'Given the reliance upon this data, it would be extremely useful to include' such validation. This indicates uncertainty about the accuracy of the modeling approach.

result: Powerful synergistic effects were observed between numerous nanobody pairs, with dramatic potency increases: S1-23 + S1-1 (~32-fold and ~21-fold), S1-RBD-15 + S1-23 (~300-fold for S1-23), S1-49 + S1-1 (>1000-fold), and S2-10-dimer with S1-23 or S1-RBD-15 (>4000-fold).
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged 'synergistic activities using nanobody cocktails' as a contribution. However, Reviewer 3 noted 'the 2D response assay has not been well adopted in antibody literature' and questioned whether strong synergy is 'unique to nanobodies, but not to human IgG antibodies,' citing contradictory literature (ter Meulen et al. 2006). Reviewer 3 also noted the >4000-fold increase for S2-10-dimer 'is not apparent from the figure' and questioned whether data refers to monomers or dimers. These concerns indicate uncertainty about the interpretation and uniqueness of the synergy findings.
